# Lomahaṁsajātaka (Ja 94)
**ID:** Ja 94
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Lomahaṁsajātaka* (Ja 94), translated as "Hair-raising", opens with the verse beginning *Sotatto sosito* [Fausböll 1877; SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha delivered this discourse while residing near Vesālī at the Pāṭikārāma in connection with Sunakkhatta [Fausböll 1877; SuttaCentral]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta lived ninety-one aeons ago as a naked ascetic (*ājīvika*) practicing extreme austerities [Fausböll 1877; Sarao and Long 2017; Anālayo 2017]. Living as a naked ascetic represented a false path stemming from wrong view, but as he lay dying, the Bodhisatta perceived a vision of hell (*nirayanimitta*); recognizing the futility of his ascetic vows, he immediately abandoned that view, took up right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), and secured rebirth in the heavenly realms [Fausböll 1877; Appleton 2010].
In Theravāda doctrinal works and the *Jātakanidānakathā*, the *Lomahaṁsajātaka* is revered as the preeminent illustration of the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhāpāramī*) [Lakshmi Narasu 1907; Gaffney 2003; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. The verses associated with this tale describe the Bodhisatta lodging in cemeteries using skeletons as pillows, maintaining an unwavering mind whether tormented and mocked by village youth or presented with garlands and scents [Gaffney 2003; War Yar Mein Da 2015]. Burmese epigraphic and art-historical records also record glosses for Jātaka 94 under the term *ājīvaka* at the Myinkaba Kubyauk-gyi temple in Pagan [Luce et al. 1970].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral identify the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta* (MN 12) as a primary canonical parallel [SuttaCentral]. Scholars observe that both texts share the same narrative occasion concerning Sunakkhatta's disparagement and depict the identical repertoire of severe former austerities, with Ja 94 explicitly situating them in a past life [Sarao and Long 2017; Anālayo 2017]. The descriptor "hair-raising" (*lomahaṁsa*) mirrors the Sanskrit title *Romaharṣaṇa-sūtra* from the *Dīrgha-āgama*, its Chinese Āgama parallel, and references in the *Milindapañha* [Anālayo 2017]. Oskar von Hinüber also notes close stylistic and formulaic prose correspondence between this Jātaka and parallel canonical discourses [von Hinüber 1994]. DharmaNexus reports no automated Pali-internal or cross-language matches above the significance threshold [DharmaNexus].
